source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality
finding: Defines the Take The Best (TTB) algorithm: recognition principle first, then cues in order of validity, stop at the first cue that discriminates, choose the object it favours. Built on Simon's satisficing. Search rule, stopping rule and decision rule are the three building blocks.
numbers: Five steps: recognition principle, search for cue values, discrimination rule, cue-substitution (stop at first discriminating cue, else try next cue), maximizing rule (guess if no cue discriminates).
limits: Needs a known cue order and binary cues. The cue order is assumed, not learned, in this paper.
agent_relevance: A cheap one-reason gate (S0) can be written as code: order checks by validity, stop at the first decisive one.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality
finding: Test environment: which of two German cities is larger, with 9 binary cues plus recognition. Simulated people with limited knowledge of cities and of cue values.
numbers: Cities above 100,000 inhabitants (text says 83; later papers use 81 objects). 9 cues; ecological validities from 1.00 (national capital, discrimination rate .02) down to .51 (East Germany, rate .27). 6 cue-knowledge levels (0,10,20,50,75,100%) x 84 recognition levels x 500 simulated persons x 3,403 city pairs = about 858 million tests. Recognition validity set to about 80% from a survey of University of Chicago students.
limits: One environment only (city size), one criterion. Simulated, not human, knowledge states.
agent_relevance: Shows how to test a simple rule by exhaustive simulation against stronger rivals; we can do the same for gate rules.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality
finding: Less-is-more effect in TTB: accuracy peaked when only part of the cities were recognized, not when all were.
numbers: Maximum about 77% correct, reached at partial knowledge (inverted U over number of cities recognized). With recognition only (0% cue values known) the peak is 65%: about half the pairs use recognition (80% correct) and the rest are guesses (50%).
limits: The effect depends on recognition validity (.80) being set high in advance. Later work found it is small and not always found (see a20).
agent_relevance: More input is not always better. An agent that reads everything may do worse than one that stops at a decisive cue.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality
finding: The competition: TTB vs five integration algorithms (tallying, weighted tallying, unit-weight linear, weighted linear, multiple regression). TTB matched the best and looked up the least.
numbers: Mean proportion correct over knowledge levels (Table 2): TTB .658; weighted tallying .658; regression .657; tallying .656; weighted linear .623; unit-weight linear .621. With 100% of cue values known: TTB .691, weighted tallying .693, regression .694. Cue values looked up: TTB 5.91 on average; integration algorithms look up all.
limits: Tested on the same 3,403 pairs it was simulated on, so not cross-validated prediction. Authors admit the integration algorithms may not be the best possible (regression on ranks did slightly better).
agent_relevance: Sets the baseline claim: one-reason search can equal full integration at a fraction of the lookups.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality
finding: Why the two linear models lost: they did not honour the recognition principle. Giving them the recognition principle instead of a recognition cue removed the whole gap.
numbers: Weighted linear .623 and unit-weight .621 vs TTB .658. Tallying algorithms ignore negative information, so they respect recognition implicitly. Authors reran with the recognition principle in the linear models: the gap disappeared.
limits: So part of the headline is the recognition principle, not the stopping rule. A fair reading: TTB equals tallying and regression here, it does not beat them.
agent_relevance: Check what really drives a win before copying a heuristic into the schema.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality
finding: Two cheaper variants: Take The Last (try the cue that discriminated last time) and Minimalist (random cue order). Both lose only a little.
numbers: Mean proportion correct: Minimalist .647; Take The Last .645 (vs TTB .658). Cue values looked up: Take The Last 5.29, Minimalist 5.64, TTB 5.91. Minimalist did about 4 points worse than TTB at some knowledge levels.
limits: Minimalist and Take The Last can give intransitive inferences (A>B, B>C, C>A) when knowledge is missing.
agent_relevance: Even a random cue order with early stopping gets most of the accuracy: stopping matters more than order.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality
finding: Transitivity and linear fit: TTB itself is transitive. Variants with random cue order can break transitivity when cue values are missing, yet accuracy stays close.
numbers: A multiple regression on the same data gave R-squared = .87, so a linear model fits well, yet the simpler nonlinear TTB matched its accuracy. Minimalist overall performance about 1 point below the best transitive algorithms.
limits: Good linear fit does not show people use linear integration.
agent_relevance: A classical rationality axiom can be violated with little accuracy cost. Do not enforce it as a guardrail where it costs compute.

source: Gigerenzer & Brighton (2009) Homo heuristicus: why biased minds make better inferences
finding: Cross-validation over 20 data sets (Czerlinski, Gigerenzer & Goldstein 1999, as reported here): tallying and take-the-best predict better out of sample than multiple regression, though regression fits better in sample.
numbers: 20 studies, 95% CIs about plus or minus .4 points. TTB looks up 2.4 cues on average; regression and tallying look up 7.7. Experienced decision theorists guessed in talks that TTB would be 5 to 10 points worse than regression, with no guess in favour of TTB.
limits: The accuracy bars are in a figure whose values were not in the extracted text, so exact percentages are not recorded here. Data sets are small paired comparisons with binary or ordinal cues.
agent_relevance: Out-of-sample testing is what makes simple rules look good. Our harness must score on held-out items for the same reason.

source: Czerlinski, Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1999) How good are simple heuristics? (as reported in Gigerenzer & Brighton 2009)
finding: Foundational cross-validation of TTB and tallying against regression over 20 real data sets. Known only through the 2009 review; the original chapter was not opened.
numbers: 20 data sets (10 from Weisberg 1985), all paired comparisons, for example which of two Chicago high schools has the higher dropout rate. Ranking: TTB and tallying above multiple regression out of sample.
limits: Secondary report only. Half of the data sets come from one textbook.
agent_relevance: Source to open next if exact percentages are needed.

source: Gigerenzer & Brighton (2009) Homo heuristicus: why biased minds make better inferences
finding: Chater et al. (2003) found TTB beat or matched a backprop network, nearest-neighbour, GCM and C4.5 when training sets were up to 40% of objects. Brighton (2006) reanalysed with cross-validation: TTB beat all rivals at every sample size.
numbers: City-size task. Chater et al. fitted on the learning sample and tested on the whole sample, which favours overfitters at large samples. With cross-validation TTB exceeded perceptron, nearest neighbour, C4.5 and CART over the full range of training sizes. Brighton (2006) reports the same across 20 data sets.
limits: Result is for the authors' own group reanalysis. It holds for small to moderate training samples and small cue sets; with large samples flexible models catch up.
agent_relevance: Simple rules win when data are scarce. Few-shot or small-sample steps of the schema are the natural home.

source: Gigerenzer & Brighton (2009) Homo heuristicus: why biased minds make better inferences
finding: The theory for why: bias-variance decomposition. Error = bias squared + variance + noise. A rule that ignores cue dependencies has high bias but low variance, so it can win on small samples. 'Overfitting' is a shorthand for variance.
numbers: Polynomial demo: fitting samples of 30 noisy observations. Higher degree always fits better, but prediction error rises past degree 3. A greedy TTB variant (cues ordered by conditional validity) fits better but predicts worse than plain TTB in the city task and in Guttman environments.
limits: Bias-variance is exact for squared error; for classification it is a metaphor.
agent_relevance: Explains when to simplify: when evidence is thin relative to model flexibility. Supports a sample-size trigger for simple mode.

source: Gigerenzer & Brighton (2009) Homo heuristicus: why biased minds make better inferences
finding: Environment structures where TTB is provably good: noncompensatory cue weights, independent cues with an odds condition, and highly redundant cues.
numbers: Noncompensatory: if each cue weight exceeds the sum of all later weights, TTB and the linear model give identical inferences (Martignon & Hoffrage 1999, 2002). Independent cues plus odds condition: TTB is optimal (Katsikopoulos & Martignon 2006). Redundant cues: TTB rivals or beats a confirmation-rule heuristic (Dieckmann & Rieskamp 2007).
limits: Unbiased is not the same as accurate. In a binary environment with zero bias, TTB was worse than its greedy counterpart on prediction.
agent_relevance: Gives checkable conditions: if our checks have steeply decaying validity, a first-decisive-check rule is safe.

source: Gigerenzer & Brighton (2009) Homo heuristicus: why biased minds make better inferences
finding: Individual-level tests of TTB and why group tests mislead. Newell, Weston & Shanks (2003) found adherence to TTB rules of 75%, 80%, 89% (Exp 1) and 92%, 89%, 89% (Exp 2), yet reported only 33% of participants fully consistent (90% cut).
numbers: Newell & Shanks (2003): validities .80, .75, .70, .69; 60 trials with feedback; only 3 of 16 participants searched in validity order. The authors argue 60 trials are too few to learn the order of the last two cues (it takes 100 or more).
limits: Critics (Newell 2005) call evidence for TTB 'elusive'. This rebuttal is by the theory's own authors. Fair reading: heterogeneity is large and adherence depends on the cut chosen.
agent_relevance: People use simple rules only some of the time. Mode choice should be conditional, as in the schema.

source: Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier (2011) Heuristic decision making, Annu Rev Psychol
finding: Fast-and-frugal trees (FFTs): binary classification trees with m+1 leaves and an exit at every node. Same building blocks as TTB. Martignon et al. (2008) tested FFTs on 30 classification problems.
numbers: Complex benchmarks including logistic regression fit better, but FFT cross-validated accuracy was close or identical. Pneumonia macrolide tree (age, fever duration) scored 72% vs 75% for a logistic score (Fischer et al. 2002).
limits: Review by authors from the same programme. The 30-problem study itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: FFTs give a transparent decision form that a code gate could implement and audit.

source: Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier (2011) Heuristic decision making, Annu Rev Psychol
finding: Coronary care unit triage (Green & Mehr 1997, as reported): a three-question FFT beat a logistic regression instrument that needed about 50 probabilities.
numbers: The tree sent fewer true heart-attack patients to a regular bed and about halved the physicians' high false-alarm rate. The regression instrument (HDPI) needed a chart and a calculator.
limits: Reported secondhand in a review; source not opened. Field data, not randomized.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a short ordered checklist can match a heavy model in a high-stakes screen.

source: Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier (2011) Heuristic decision making, Annu Rev Psychol
finding: Bail decisions (Dhami 2003, as reported): a fast-and-frugal tree predicted London magistrates' bail decisions better than a weighted additive model.
numbers: Two courts: tree 92% and 85% correct (cross-validated) vs 86% and 73% for weighted additive. Magistrates spent 6 to 10 minutes per case yet said they weighed everything.
limits: Describes behaviour, not whether the decisions were right. Reported secondhand.
agent_relevance: Stated reasoning and actual decision rule can differ; fits our guardrail that written reasoning is not a record of how a decision was made.

source: Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier (2011) Heuristic decision making, Annu Rev Psychol
finding: Hiatus heuristic vs Pareto/NBD (Wuebben & Wangenheim 2008, as reported): a one-cue recency rule classified active customers as well or better than the state-of-the-art statistical model.
numbers: Apparel retailer 83% vs 75%; airline 77% vs 74%; online CD retailer tie at 77%. Pareto/NBD fitted on 40 weeks and tested on the next 40; the hiatus rule has no parameters (9 months for retailer and airline, 6 for CD).
limits: Three firms; one tie. Reported secondhand.
agent_relevance: A zero-parameter rule can beat a fitted model when fitted parameters add variance. Relevant to gate rules with no fitted weights.

source: Pachur, Todd, Gigerenzer, Schooler & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a review of theory and tests
finding: Recognition heuristic (RH): if exactly one of two objects is recognized, infer it has the higher criterion value. It is ecologically rational when recognition validity (alpha) is high. The review covers four claims: recognition is a valid cue, people follow it, it is noncompensatory, and it yields less-is-more.
numbers: Alpha = C/(C+W) over pairs with exactly one recognized object. Across 11 studies the correlation between alpha and the share of judgements following RH was r = .64 (reported in Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier 2011). Swiss cities: alpha .86 for population vs .51 for distance from center; accordance 89% vs 54% (Pohl 2006).
limits: Accordance rates are group means; strategy use varies across individuals. The domain must be a coherent reference class: mixing real and fictitious objects breaks prediction.
agent_relevance: A familiarity-first gate is valid only where a familiarity signal correlates with the answer. The agent must check alpha for its domain.

source: Pachur, Todd, Gigerenzer, Schooler & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a review of theory and tests
finding: Boundary conditions from partial or failed replications: contradicting cues reduce use of RH; mixed or unknown reference classes lower it; conclusive criterion knowledge makes it unnecessary.
numbers: Pohl (2006): 89% accordance with a consistent set of large cities vs 75% in a mixed set. Oppenheimer (2003): recognized small nearby towns vs fictitious cities, recognized city chosen only 37% of the time. Richter & Spaeth data: 17 of 28 participants followed RH with zero or one exceptions in 32 trials even when told the recognized city had no international airport.
limits: Authors defend RH as adaptive; critics (Oppenheimer, Hilbig) read the same data as compensatory use. Individual-level reanalysis (Pachur et al. 2008): about half of participants follow RH on every trial.
agent_relevance: Heuristics fail when the agent has direct, conclusive knowledge. A gate should defer to a verified fact over a heuristic prior.

source: Pachur, Todd, Gigerenzer, Schooler & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a review of theory and tests
finding: Less-is-more for recognition is mixed in tests: found in some, absent in others. Katsikopoulos (2010) shows it can occur without alpha > beta under imperfect memory.
numbers: Pachur (2010) reviewed 10 data sets where recognition validity exceeded knowledge validity and concluded evidence was mixed. Found by Goldstein & Gigerenzer (2002), Frosch et al. (2007) and in groups (Reimer & Katsikopoulos 2004); not found by Pachur & Biele (2007) or Pohl (2006).
limits: Effect is predicted to be small and depends on hit and false-alarm rates of recognition memory (Pleskac 2007). Absence is not clean evidence against RH use (Hilbig et al. 2010).
agent_relevance: Do not build the schema on 'less information improves accuracy'. Build it on 'extra information is not guaranteed to help'.

source: Pachur, Todd, Gigerenzer, Schooler & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a review of theory and tests
finding: Memory models give alternative accounts: ACT-R forgetting produces less-is-more (Schooler & Hertwig 2005); MINERVA with continuous familiarity also produces it (Dougherty et al. 2008); a two-high-threshold model explains response-time data that had been read as compensatory use (Erdfelder et al. 2011).
numbers: Schooler & Hertwig add the fluency heuristic (use recognition speed when both objects are recognized). Collective recognition correlates with real quantities in sports, stocks and cities.
limits: Threshold vs continuous recognition debate unresolved. Broeder & Schuetz reanalysis of 59 studies (as reported in Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier 2011): threshold models fit better in about half.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: the effect may come from a graded familiarity signal, not a yes/no one. Our uncertainty signal should be graded.

source: Pachur, Todd, Gigerenzer, Schooler & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a review of theory and tests
finding: Wimbledon forecasting with recognition: amateurs' recognition beat expert rankings (Serwe & Frings 2006, as reported).
numbers: RH correct on 73% of matches where it applied; collective recognition 72%; ATP Entry Ranking 66%, ATP Champions Race 68%, Wimbledon seeding 69% (2003 tournament). Scheibehenne & Broeder (2007) reported a similar result for 2006.
limits: One tournament at a time. Recognition by German amateurs partly reflects nationality.
agent_relevance: A cheap ignorance-based signal can beat expert-built rankings in noisy forecasting.

source: Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier (2011) Heuristic decision making, Annu Rev Psychol
finding: Recognition-based investing and elections: mixed evidence (as reported).
numbers: Ortmann et al. (2008): recognition portfolios on average beat managed funds, the market, chance portfolios and experts. Boyd (2001): no advantage using college students' recognition. German elections: recognition forecasts almost as accurate as vote-intention surveys (Gaissmaier & Marewski 2010).
limits: Reported secondhand. Authors call the finance result an open question.
agent_relevance: Heuristic wins are domain-specific; require a domain check before trusting.

source: Phillips, Neth, Woike & Gaissmaier (2017) FFTrees: a toolbox to create, visualize, and evaluate fast-and-frugal decision trees
finding: Formal and computational model of FFTs: the fan algorithms (ifan, dfan) build a set of trees with different exit structures and pick one by weighted accuracy; max and zig-zag are older construction rules. Implemented in the FFTrees R package.
numbers: Ten real data sets; 100 simulations per data set; 50% train, 50% test. Mean cues used: fan 1.85, zig-zag 4.85, max 6.5. Mean balanced accuracy of construction rules: fan .81, zig-zag .75, max .64. Median build time ifan 2.61 s vs 0.59 s for max.
limits: Toolbox authors chose the ten data sets; max and zig-zag are weak baselines.
agent_relevance: Gives an executable FFT builder; a gate could be learned from our own benchmark items with this method.

source: Phillips, Neth, Woike & Gaissmaier (2017) FFTrees: a toolbox to create, visualize, and evaluate fast-and-frugal decision trees
finding: FFTs compete with machine-learning classifiers on out-of-sample balanced accuracy while using about two cues.
numbers: Mean prediction balanced accuracy over data sets: SVM .86 (crashed on arrhythmia and audiology, so not like-for-like), FFT .83, regularized logistic regression .83, random forest .83. FFT did worst relative to others on the occupancy data set (.96). Arrhythmia (68 cases, 280 cues): FFT .66, CART .64, LR .52, RLR .70, NB .71, RF .69.
limits: Not all methods were tuned equally; small data sets favour FFT.
agent_relevance: Where cases are few and cues many, a short tree is a competitive fallback.

source: Phillips, Neth, Woike & Gaissmaier (2017) FFTrees: a toolbox to create, visualize, and evaluate fast-and-frugal decision trees
finding: Frugality and speed measures for tree-style heuristics: mean cues used (mcu) and percent cues ignored (pci); a signal-detection view with sensitivity, specificity and bias set by where exits sit.
numbers: Heart-disease example: the tree uses about 1.7 cues on average; weighted accuracy about .88 in training and test; cue costs are explicit (for example thal $102.90, cp $1.00) so a cheap-first tree can be built by cost.
limits: One data set (heart disease). Costs are illustrative.
agent_relevance: Our gates can be scored by cues used and by the balance of misses vs false alarms, not by accuracy alone.

source: Bobadilla-Suarez & Love (2018) Fast or frugal, but not both: decision heuristics under time pressure
finding: Frugal is not the same as fast. TTB uses fewer cues than tallying but was slower and worse under time pressure when stimuli invited a sequential search. The effect reversed when the display cut search cost.
numbers: Experiment 1: TTB slower and less compliant under time pressure than tallying. Experiment 2 (reformatted stimuli): reverse pattern. Participants were told which heuristic to follow; task was which country has higher GDP. Exact reaction times and N not extracted.
limits: Instructed heuristics, not spontaneous choice; inference from givens, not from memory; a speed-accuracy trade-off clouds one result (TTB compliance higher on harder trials).
agent_relevance: For an LLM, count the real cost (calls, tokens), not the number of cues. A sequential lookup can cost more than a parallel sum.

source: Schulz, Speekenbrink & Meder (2016) Simple trees in complex forests: growing Take The Best by approximate Bayesian computation
finding: Computational account of how TTB can be learned: Polya-urn style reinforcement of cue order and direction, accepting proposal trees that predict a data subset (ABC-TTB).
numbers: City data: 81 objects, 9 binary cues. Compared TTB, ABC-TTB and CART across learning-set sizes from 5 objects up; ABC-TTB performed best overall (read from a figure; exact accuracies not extracted). Compute rises faster than exponentially as the acceptance standard tightens.
limits: Proof of concept on one data set. Cost of learning is not counted in the accuracy comparison.
agent_relevance: Shows heuristic structure can be learned from experience rather than prespecified, a route to learn our gate order from run logs.

source: Peltola, Jokinen & Kaski (2019) Probabilistic formulation of the Take The Best heuristic
finding: TTB written as a likelihood model with a noise term, so cue order, direction and discrimination thresholds can be fitted by MCMC and uncertainty is explicit.
numbers: Four benchmark data sets (homeless, profsalary, city, mileage), 1000 train/test splits. Probabilistic TTB performed comparably or better than classic TTB and ABC-TTB, and better than logistic regression except on mileage (the largest data set).
limits: Four data sets only; accuracy curves read from a figure.
agent_relevance: Gives a calibrated version of one-reason choice, useful when the gate must output a probability and not a hard stop.

source: Jagadish, Thalmann, Coda-Forno, Binz & Schulz (2026, v3) Meta-learning ecological priors from large language models explains human learning and decision making
finding: Uses an LLM to generate about 7,000 decision tasks per condition, meta-learns a network on them, and the network picks the same heuristics people do: one-reason when cue ranking is known, equal weights when direction is known, weighted when neither is known.
numbers: Gini of attribute weights: ranking condition M = .3399 (SEM .0631, one-reason); direction condition .0743 (SEM .0138, equal weighting); unknown condition .1794 (SEM .0333, weighted). Best account of human choices by posterior model frequency: .7299 (2-attribute experiment) and .6284 (4-attribute), beating single-cue, equal-weight, feedforward net and meta-learned inference with a hand-built prior.
limits: The LLM generates task environments; it is not itself tested as a decision maker. Human data come from one earlier study (Binz et al.). Preprint.
agent_relevance: Suggests strategy choice should follow what is known about cue structure (order known, direction known, or neither). That is a testable rule for our mode selector.

source: Bogdan (2026) Free energy heuristics: fast-and-frugal cognition as active inference under uncertain precision
finding: Claims a theorem that an agent unsure of the precision of its own evidence should truncate cue integration after a finite number of high-validity cues, and under a Descending Dominance condition this equals take-the-best. Tests the prediction on LLMs: longer chain of thought lowers accuracy on unanswerable (Knightian) items.
numbers: FEH-79 benchmark; the confirmatory run used 45 items (31 high-uncertainty: 20 forecasts, 9 novel-synthetic, 2 strategic; 14 controls). 7 models (phi3.5 3.8B, Mistral 7B, Qwen2.5 7B/14B/32B, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5), 5 reasoning-length conditions, 5 replications = 7,875 cells. High-uncertainty accuracy: 77.1% direct, then 66.5%, 64.7%, 64.4%, 62.1% with longer reasoning (pooled drop 12.7 points). Controls about 82% and flat (drop 1.73). Pre-registered hierarchical estimate: 17.3-point drop, 95% CrI [7.7, 25.5], posterior 1.00.
limits: Single author, preprint. 'Correct' means choosing the offered 'cannot be determined' option, so the task rewards recognizing indeterminacy, not predicting well. Effect decisive in the three Qwen models, directional in the two frontier models, reversed in phi3.5 and inconclusive in Mistral. A maximal random-slope variant fell just under the registered threshold. The item pool is dated and tied to one provider panel.
agent_relevance: Bears on G1: on questions with no settled answer, more written reasoning may lower accuracy. The evidence is weak (scoring choice, frontier models not clear). Test on our own tasks before adopting a rule.

source: Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier (2011) Heuristic decision making, Annu Rev Psychol
finding: Ecological rationality as the unifying idea: a heuristic is good or bad relative to an environment structure, not in the abstract. The adaptive toolbox is a set of building blocks (search, stopping, decision rules) combined for the task.
numbers: Tallying wins at low predictability (R-squared about .5 or less), few objects per cue (ratio 10 or less) and correlated cues (Einhorn & Hogarth 1975, as reported in Gigerenzer & Brighton 2009). Recognition validity predicts reliance on recognition (r = .64 over 11 studies).
limits: Single research programme. Critics (Hogarth, Newell, Dougherty, Oppenheimer) argue many results are task-specific or explained by compensatory models; their papers were not opened here.
agent_relevance: Give the schema an explicit environment test (validity spread, redundancy, sample size) before choosing simple vs full mode.
